I feel like there are a lot of different ways to think about this question, including what constitutes "digital" and "writing" ...
What are the benefits and constraints of digital writing?
That's the thing I'm wondering about too: what is digital writing? The next question is what recommends it?

I'm not sure I exactly get what you mean by "recommends" - do you mean what things require it? If so, I'm not sure I have a concrete answer. For me, I try to use technologies in ways that get to interesting questions, rather than focusing on the technology (although maybe the use of Voat was designed to be a little provocative that way).

By "recommends it" I am wondering what inspires the use of it. I just built a shelf last week and there were a couple of oddly angled cuts I needed to make. I could have gone to my brother's house and used his chop saw which can be set for whatever angle I could need. Instead, I clamped guides onto the wood and cut it by hand. Two things recommended the handsaw: I had it in my house so I didn't need to drive across town and there is a certain feel to cutting things by hand that I like more than using an electric device. It was, for lack of a better word, human.

So, what recommends this as a way of writing? It's a way of discussing, but of creation, I'm not so sure.

I would argue that writing is an emergent process, and so discussion is always a kind of writing culture (a small culture in this case), but I see your point about this not being a usually validated kind of creative practice.

There can be lost communication in communicating digitally. We are all sitting in the same room not having a conversation. Yet we are having a conversation with our minds and hands. Weird? Or the new millennium?

Yeah, there's an artificiality to it as we practice things here. I mean, why am I not just saying this to you. But when we are at distance, that's another matter.

So, is this at all useful in a classroom when we could just talk to one another? Does it give voice to some who would be quiet in other forms of discussion?

For my part, I'd say this can function well in a classroom, although honestly this is a bit of an experiment too - maybe that's obvious given some of the tech hiccups. But I wonder how this would work with 20+ people talking instead of just 5?

Mainly, I think your last question gets to it. Some people are more comfortable writing, especially in an informal space. Sort of like opening up a google doc and letting people type instead of speak in a classroom discussion.

Well, I see it is a sped-up (and somewhat stripped down) version of how publishing books and newspaper articles used to work - lots of people never physically speaking but doing a lot of conversing through text.

I'm actually interested in having a bigger conversation about what "digital" means. Angela Haas, in her article "Wampum as Hypertext," makes the argument that "digital" writing is anything pertaining to the digits - that is, anything done with fingers.

For my part, I don't think that it has to be published necessarily, just written with something other than a pen on paper. Even that definition is a little narrow, though - I have a really broad idea of what "writing" is, I guess?

Ok, yeah, this stuff, Gina, about having a (digital) audience that is different from a (regular or analog) audience -- well, that's very interesting to me. In fact, that question is center stage for this whole medium. Thanks for bringing it up. Sometimes I think that having an audience is a fiction. An audience is mostly an idea, a picture I have in my head. Right now, for instance, I can't be sure who is reading my comment, and if anyone is, I don't know what they think. So I have to imagine, just about at every sentence, how my words might be taken (and mis-taken). But here's the thing: 90% of the time, it doesn't matter. The imaginative act of creating an audience is really crucial for me because it helps me generate ideas and see the relationship between ideas. Even writing to myself in my journal sort of makes me think about the way I"m being read. I can't help it. It's like looking in a mirror when I pass it. Pants on frontwards? Check. But then, when it becomes digital, I can get comments that make me feel I'm being read -- and maybe that is, and this sounds very shallow, I know, but maybe that is all that matters sometimes. Having a deep critique or a generative analysis is great, but that's hard to do on such media as this. So maybe digital media are our mirrors. And others wave to us from the other side. And we sign. Smile. And then?
